stem: The main aim of supply-side policy is to

options.content: increase the level of consumer spending in the economy
options.rationale: That would shift aggregate demand, which is demand-side policy.

options.content: increase the productive capacity of the economy
options.rationale: Correct: it shifts the LRAS curve to the right.

options.content: reduce the government's budget deficit in the short run
options.rationale: That is a fiscal objective, not the aim of supply-side policy.

options.content: fix the exchange rate against the currencies of trading partners
options.rationale: That is exchange rate policy.

explanation: Supply-side policy raises potential output by improving the quantity, quality or efficiency of resources.

stem: Which of the following is an example of supply-side policy?

options.content: A government grant to colleges for vocational training
options.rationale: Correct: it improves the skills of the labour force.

options.content: A cut in the central bank's policy interest rate
options.rationale: This is monetary policy that raises demand.

options.content: A rise in the pensions paid to retired workers
options.rationale: This is a transfer payment that raises demand.

options.content: A temporary cut in the rate of value added tax
options.rationale: This mainly raises aggregate demand.

explanation: Training raises human capital and productivity, shifting LRAS to the right.

stem: A successful supply-side policy, with no change in aggregate demand, is most likely to cause

options.content: a rise in real GDP and a rise in the price level
options.rationale: A rise in AD would do this, not a rise in supply.

options.content: a fall in real GDP and a fall in the price level
options.rationale: Output rises when capacity rises.

options.content: a fall in real GDP and a rise in the price level
options.rationale: This is the effect of a fall in supply (cost-push).

options.content: a rise in real GDP and a fall in the price level
options.rationale: Correct: SRAS shifts to the right along a downward-sloping AD curve.

explanation: A rightward shift of SRAS lowers the price level and raises real output.
hints: Draw SRAS shifting right along a fixed AD curve.

stem: How might deregulation raise aggregate supply?

options.content: By increasing the rate of income tax paid by firms
options.rationale: A tax rise would raise costs, not lower them.

options.content: By reducing the supply of credit to new firms
options.rationale: This would restrict supply.

options.content: By lowering the costs of starting and running businesses
options.rationale: Correct: fewer licences and less red tape reduce costs.

options.content: By raising the minimum wage above the market wage
options.rationale: This is intervention that raises labour costs.

explanation: Removing unnecessary rules lowers costs and encourages new firms, so supply rises.

stem: Which supply-side policy is likely to have the LONGEST time lag?

options.content: Cutting the rate of tax on company profits
options.rationale: Firms can respond within a year or two.

options.content: Reforming schools and colleges to raise skills
options.rationale: Correct: a new generation must be educated before productivity rises.

options.content: Reducing the paperwork needed to register a business
options.rationale: This can take effect quite quickly.

options.content: Giving a one-year allowance for new machinery
options.rationale: Firms can respond during the year.

explanation: Education and infrastructure take years; tax incentives and deregulation act more quickly.
hints: Which policy needs people to complete years of study?

options.rationale: Correct: output per worker rises from 92 to 104, a rise of 13.04%.
This is the rise in output per worker (12 units), not a percentage.
This divides the rise by the new level (12 ÷ 104) instead of the original.

hints: Productivity is output per worker; find it before and after.

stem: Why might supply-side policy fail to reduce unemployment in the short run?

options.content: Supply-side policy always raises the price level and so reduces employment
options.rationale: A successful policy lowers or stabilises the price level.

options.content: Supply-side policy has no effect on the productivity of labour
options.rationale: Training and technology raise productivity.

options.content: Training takes years to work, and jobs will not appear if demand is weak
options.rationale: Correct: lags and weak demand limit the effect.

options.content: Unemployment is caused only by the level of the minimum wage
options.rationale: Unemployment has many causes.

explanation: The effects are slow, and structural unemployment will remain if there are too few vacancies.
hints: Think about lags and the demand for labour.

stem: A factory employs 120 workers who together produce 10,800 units a month. Calculate labour productivity, in units per worker per month.
explanation: Productivity = 10,800 ÷ 120 = 90 units per worker.

stem: Define supply-side policy.

points.description: Government policies that aim to raise the productive capacity of the economy.
By increasing the quantity, quality or efficiency of resources, so shifting the long-run aggregate supply curve to the right.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Supply-side policy consists of government policies that aim to raise the productive capacity of the economy by increasing the quantity, quality or efficiency of resources, which shifts the long-run aggregate supply curve to the right.

explanation: Aim of capacity; mechanism through resources and LRAS.
hints: Mention capacity and the AS curve.

stem: Explain how government spending on training could shift the long-run aggregate supply curve to the right.

points.description: Training raises the skills of the labour force (human capital).
So output per worker (productivity) rises.
Workers are better matched to vacancies, so structural unemployment falls and more resources are employed.
Potential output rises, so LRAS shifts to the right.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Training raises the skills of the labour force, so the output of each worker (productivity) rises. Workers are also better matched to the vacancies that firms have, so structural unemployment falls and more resources are used. Potential output therefore rises, so the long-run aggregate supply curve shifts to the right.

explanation: Skills, productivity, employment, LRAS.
hints: Start with the skills of workers.

stem: Explain how a cut in the rate of tax on company profits could raise aggregate supply.

points.description: Firms keep more of each dollar of profit, so the reward for investment rises.
They are likely to invest more in machinery and buildings.
The capital stock grows, which raises productive capacity.
So long-run aggregate supply shifts to the right (with a time lag).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A lower tax on profits means that firms keep more of each dollar earned, which increases the reward for investing. They are likely to invest more in machinery and buildings, so the capital stock grows and productive capacity rises. Long-run aggregate supply therefore shifts to the right, although this takes time.

explanation: Incentive, investment, capacity, LRAS with lag.

stem: Analyse why supply-side policies often have long time lags.

points.description: Education and training take years to produce a skilled labour force.
Building roads, power stations and railways takes years of planning and construction.
Firms respond to incentives only after they have planned and carried out investment.
Research and new technology take time to develop and to spread through the economy.
So the shift in LRAS happens slowly, and the policy cannot cure a short-run recession.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Education and training take years to produce a skilled labour force, and roads, railways and power stations take years to plan and build. Firms respond to tax incentives only after they have planned and carried out new investment, and new technology takes time to develop and spread. The shift in long-run aggregate supply therefore happens slowly, so supply-side policy cannot cure a short-run recession.

explanation: Lags for education, infrastructure, investment, technology; consequence.
hints: Compare how quickly each policy works.

stem:
**A training programme at a Gweru clothing firm (fictional, illustrative)**

A clothing firm in Gweru employs 200 workers and makes 16,000 shirts a month. The government pays half the cost of a training programme in modern sewing methods. After the programme the same 200 workers make 18,400 shirts a month. Wages are unchanged.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate labour productivity before the training, in shirts per worker.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate labour productivity after the training, in shirts per worker.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage rise in labour productivity, as a percentage.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain how a rise in productivity across many firms could lead to a lower price level in the economy.

points.description: Output per worker rises while wages do not, so labour cost per unit falls.
Lower costs of production shift the short-run aggregate supply curve to the right.
At the existing level of demand, firms can sell more at a lower price.
So the price level falls, or rises more slowly, and real output rises.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: If output per worker rises while wages do not, the labour cost of each unit falls. Lower costs of production shift the short-run aggregate supply curve to the right. With aggregate demand unchanged, firms can sell more at a lower price, so the price level falls (or rises more slowly) and real output rises.

explanation: Productivity rises from 80 to 92 shirts per worker, 15%; lower unit costs shift AS right.

stem:
**Roads and power in Mbira (a fictional economy, illustrative)**

Mbira's firms face high transport costs and frequent power cuts. The government plans to spend on rural roads, electricity generation and a training scheme for technicians. Officials estimate that, when complete, the programme will raise the quantity of real GDP supplied by US\$160 million at every price level. The spending will take about six years and will be paid for by a small rise in taxes.

| Price level (index) | AD (US\$ million) | SRAS before (US\$ million) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 60 | 1,135 | 810 |
| 70 | 1,050 | 890 |
| 80 | 970 | 970 |
| 90 | 890 | 1,030 |
| 100 | 810 | 1,070 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: After the programme is complete, find the new equilibrium level of real GDP, in US\$ million.
parts.explanation: SRAS after = SRAS before + 160. At a price level of 70, 890 + 160 = 1,050, which equals AD (1,050): equilibrium real GDP is US\$1,050 million.
parts.workedSolution: 1. SRAS after = SRAS before + 160. At a price level of 70, 890 + 160 = 1,050, which equals AD (1,050): equilibrium real GDP is US\$1,050 million.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage change in the price level between the old and new equilibrium, to one decimal place. Include the minus sign if the price level falls.
parts.explanation: The price level falls from 80 to 70: (70 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = −12.5%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The price level falls from 80 to 70: (70 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = −12.5%.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how better roads and a reliable electricity supply could shift the aggregate supply curve to the right.

points.description: They lower firms' costs of transport and of standby power.
Lower costs mean firms can supply more at each price level (short-run aggregate supply shifts right).
They raise productive capacity because firms can operate for longer and reach markets, so LRAS shifts right.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Better roads and a reliable electricity supply lower firms' costs of transport and standby power, so firms can supply more at each price level and the short-run aggregate supply curve shifts to the right. They also allow firms to operate for longer and to reach more markets, which raises productive capacity and shifts the long-run aggregate supply curve to the right.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Assess whether the government's programme is a good way of improving the economy of Mbira.

points.description: Real GDP rises by US\$80 million and the price level falls by 12.5%: growth without inflation.
Lower costs make Mbira's firms more competitive.
The programme takes about six years, so it does not help in the short run.
The cost is paid by higher taxes and may reduce spending now, and benefits are uncertain.
Training may not match employers' needs; extra jobs depend on demand for output.
Judgement: worthwhile for long-term benefits if well designed and affordable.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, developed and applied to the data, with a supported judgement.
Some development of one side or limited use of the data.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: On the figures, real GDP rises by US\$80 million and the price level falls by 12.5%, which is growth without inflation, and lower costs would make Mbira's firms more competitive. However, the programme takes about six years, so it does nothing for the economy in the short run, and it is paid for by higher taxes that reduce spending now. The benefits are uncertain because the training may not match what employers need, and extra jobs depend on enough demand for the extra output. Overall it is worthwhile for the long-term benefits if it is well designed and affordable, but it should be accompanied by measures to support demand while it is built.

explanation: New equilibrium US\$1,050 million at price level 70 (−12.5%); lower costs and capacity; long lags, cost and uncertainty.
hints: Add 160 to SRAS before at each price level, then find where AD equals the new SRAS.
In (d) consider time lags, cost and the need for demand.

stem: Assess the effectiveness of supply-side policies in reducing unemployment.

points.description: Training and better job information reduce structural unemployment by matching skills to jobs.
Raising capacity and lowering costs lets firms expand and employ more.
Tax incentives and deregulation encourage firms to start up and to hire.
They can reduce unemployment without causing inflation.
Time lags are long.
Cost and uncertainty: training may not match demand for skills.
If unemployment is caused by weak aggregate demand, supply-side policy will not create jobs.
Some policies (tax cuts) may widen inequality.
Application to an economy with structural unemployment.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, developed and applied to the question, with a supported judgement.
Some development and application; evaluation limited or judgement not supported.
Simple, undeveloped points with little application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Supply-side policies such as training and better information about vacancies reduce structural unemployment by matching the skills of workers to the jobs available, and lower costs and greater capacity allow firms to expand and employ more. Tax incentives and deregulation encourage new firms to start up and to hire, and these policies can reduce unemployment without causing inflation. However, the time lags are long, because training and infrastructure take years to work, and the cost is high and the results uncertain: training may not match the skills that employers need. If unemployment is caused by weak aggregate demand, supply-side policy will not create jobs, and some policies, such as tax cuts, may widen inequality. Supply-side policy is therefore effective against structural unemployment over the long term, but it needs to be combined with demand management when unemployment is also cyclical.

explanation: Structural unemployment and non-inflationary growth against lags, cost, uncertainty and weak demand.
hints: Consider lags, cost, the type of unemployment and the level of demand.
